Q: Flexibility in defining attributes in qt strings A:

QString doesn't really have "attributes" and cannot be expanded as you might think.

Also, subclassing them in order to provide custom behavior makes little sense, as they don't have virtual functions that could be overridden.

Just make your own function

The most obvious solution would be to create a function that would return a modified string, and then simply call it within setText().

lab.setText(yesNoFix("<qt>The default value is: <code>YES</code></qt>"));

If you have full control and knowledge about the possible strings you'd get, that yesNoFix() could just be a simple function that would search for a matching string (eg: <code>YES</code>) and replace it, so that the above could eventually return a modified string including the color within the code tag.

If, otherwise, you may have complex strings, also containing other words within the code tags, or other tag attributes, the only options are to either use a function based on regexp, or one using a [x]HTML parser that would eventually find matching node patterns and replace their contents before returning the result.

Both solutions are relatively simple, but require proper care: regular expressions are not really meant for this and it's relatively common to spend time to create a reasonable pattern that could eventually break in unexpected cases, and fixing such patterns isn't immediate; on the other hand, writing a proper and reliable parser is not very efficient for a simple need like this, while using third-party libraries may not be doable or reasonable.

Using existing Qt features

Rich text capable widgets in Qt

Qt provides two text based widgets that have full rich text capabilities, but with different API and behavior: QTextEdit and QLabel.

There is also QPlainTextEdit, but it's a special case as it has only few formatting capabilities (custom fonts and colors).

Other than the obvious differences (QTextEdit is a scrollable edit field, whereas QLabel is only intended to display the whole text) the most important difference is how the contents are actually stored and accessed:

  • QTextEdit stores the text content in a QTextDocument (accessible through the document property), but even though "HTML" based content can be set using setHtml(), the "original HTML" is never stored: it is just parsed and converted into QTextDocument elements; as a consequence, the output of toHtml() is almost never the same as what was used with setHtml();

  • QLabel has a single text property that stores the "text", which may or may not contain HTML tags; the label eventually decides how to show that text depending on the fact that it "believes" it may have rich text contents (see Qt::mightBeRichText()) or depending on the textFormat property;

Both have their pros and cons:

  • QTextEdit is a scroll area, therefore it has complex mechanisms to provide appropriate size hints in layouts; "fixing" them in order to have a QTextEdit that behaves as a QLabel would in a layout (with reasonable width and height hints) is not easy, and what may seem to work fine on your tests may fail in other systems;
  • there is no public API for the rich text support used in QLabel, meaning that we have to rely on current knowledge and assumptions, which may be broken in future versions, or unexpected in previous ones, even though officially supported by your program;

Based on your original request, I will focus on QLabel in the next section, as managing size hints and interactions for QTextEdit is not really in the scope of the question.

Accessing QLabel private objects

Whenever rich text display is needed on a QLabel, it internally creates a private QWidgetTextControl QObject, which is responsible of retaining the QTextDocument used to contain the "rich text contents" and eventually accesses it when needed: to paint the text considering all formatting aspects, but also allow limited user interaction, such as clicking on a hyperlink or allow user selection through mouse or keyboard.

We need to access that QTextDocument in order to change the appearance in that behavior, and we can do it by using findChild() on the label by looking for a QTextDocument within its own object tree.

My suggestion is to create a QLabel subclass and alter its behavior whenever you need special formatting capabilities.

Note that the QTextDocument indicated above is a child of QWidgetTextControl (a Qt child of the QLabel), but that control is automatically created only when the text is not empty and one of the following is true:

  • Qt::mightBeRichText() returns true on the given text;
  • the textFormat property has been set to Qt::RichText (or Qt::MarkDownText in newer Qt versions);
  • setTextInteractionFlags() has been called with any proper Qt::TextInteractionFlag except from Qt::NoTextInteraction (avoid using Qt::TextEditable);

also note that the QWidgetTextControl object (and its child document) may also be destroyed whenever the textFormat, textInteractionFlags and the result of mightBeRichText() within setText() don't require rich text capabilities.

Since those are private objects, extreme care is needed when using or subclassing such a class, otherwise you may end up with unexpected behavior or fatal crash due to inappropriate memory access.

At this point, we know how to get access to the internal QTextDocument, meaning that we can make use of its setDefaultStyleSheet() function to set up a "global CSS" that will always be used whenever the document contents are changed.[1]

Considering the above, we can start to set our implementation by subclassing QLabel and add a few things:

from PyQt5.QtCore import *
from PyQt5.QtGui import *
from PyQt5.QtWidgets import *


class CustomLabel(QLabel):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        # clear the "text" argument, as it has to be used later
        if args and isinstance(args[0], str):
            text, *args = args
        else:
            text = ''
        if 'text' in kwargs:
            text = kwargs.pop('text')

        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)

        # necessary to ensure that the necessary objects are created
        self.setTextFormat(Qt.RichText)
        self.setText(' ')

        self._doc = self.findChild(QTextDocument)
        self._doc.setDefaultStyleSheet('code { color: blue; }')

        if text:
            # set the actual text
            self.setText(text)
        else:
            # clear the label
            self.setText('')


app = QApplication([])

test = CustomLabel('This tag contains some <code>code</code>')
test.show()

app.exec()

Note that I specifically ignored any predefined text in the constructor, I set a non empty string for its text; only then I tried to access the QTextDocument and eventually updated the text. Those steps are necessary to ensure that the QWidgetTextControl instance is created and never destroyed.[2]

The above will show something similar to this (appearance changes depending on the OS and its settings):

This can be extended by expanding the setDefaultStyleSheet() call and using appropriate tags. Note that the Qt rich text engine luckily considers unknown tags as valid CSS classes, other than respecting the id attribute, so we can even use custom-named tags as class rules:

class CustomLabel(QLabel):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        ...
        fixed = QFontDatabase.systemFont(QFontDatabase.FixedFont).family()
        self._doc.setDefaultStyleSheet((
            'code { color: blue; }'
            'code#yes, yes { color: green; }'
            'yes { font-family: FIXED; }'
            'code#no, no { color: red; }'
            'no { font-family: FIXED; }'
        ).replace('FIXED', fixed))
        ...

app = QApplication([])

test = QWidget()
lay = QVBoxLayout(test)
lay.addWidget(CustomLabel('Normal text'))
lay.addWidget(CustomLabel('Some <code>code tag</code>'))
lay.addWidget(CustomLabel('A <code>code tag with break,<br>YES and NO</code>'))
lay.addWidget(CustomLabel('A <code id="yes">code tag with "yes" id</code>'))
lay.addWidget(CustomLabel('A <yes>yes tag</yes>'))
lay.addWidget(CustomLabel('A <no>no tag</no>'))

test.show()
app.exec()

Qt uses the QFontDatabase::FixedFont enum as style hinting for fixed font tags such as code, tt, kbd, samp and pre. I used it in order to ensure that "unknown" tags would still apply the same font when using a "non-code" tag.

And here is the result:

Still, that could not be enough, as we may want different colors depending on the text within the given tags.

Further expanding with QSyntaxHighlighter

Since we are using a QTextDocument, we can take advantage of the QSyntaxHighlighter class, which allows to further extend a QTextDocument by internally changing its text formats without altering the actual document structure.

The benefit is that we can also change the appearance of the text document contents (including the formatting previously specified for it) and expand it using context-based search.

The following code shows a simple implementation of a QSyntaxHighlighter subclass which will eventually show the "YES" or "NO" words in a different color, as long as they are within a "fixed" font tag as <code>.

class Highlighter(QSyntaxHighlighter):
    codeColors = {
        'YES': QColor('green'), 
        'NO': QColor('red'), 
    }

    def highlightBlock(self, text):
        tc = QTextCursor(self.document())
        blockStart = self.currentBlock().position()
        fixed = QFontDatabase.systemFont(QFontDatabase.FixedFont).family()

        for key, color in self.codeColors.items():
            if not key in text:
                continue

            sz = len(key)
            pos = 0
            while True:
                pos = text.find(key, pos)
                if pos < 0:
                    break

                tc.setPosition(blockStart + pos + sz)
                if tc.charFormat().fontFamily() == fixed:
                    fmt = QTextCharFormat()
                    fmt.setForeground(color)
                    fmt.setFontWeight(QFont.Bold)
                    self.setFormat(pos, sz, fmt)
                pos += sz


class CustomLabel(QLabel):
    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        ...
        self._doc = self.findChild(QTextDocument)
        self._highlighter = Highlighter(self._doc)
        ...

...

Which will show the following, while using the same widgets and tags as done above:

As you can see, the "YES" and "NO" text are shown with different color and font weight.

Note that, for obvious reasons, the above has some limitations: for instance, the "YES" would be shown in green with a bold font even when using a <pre> tag, and that's because Qt doesn't differentiate such tags when parsing HTML contents. A possibility would be to extend this by using HTML tag attributes such as class or id in the original text, and make a reverse search with the QTextCorsor or the document format ranges.

[1] Although Qt uses the same internal parsers for HTML and CSS, and the same CSS parser is also used when calling setStyleSheet() on a widget or the QApplication, those functions do not apply the given QSS to the text contents of a rich text based widget: those colors are only eventually used as the default palette pen and brush when drawing text contents.
Using a class rule such as code in a QWidget::setStyleSheet() call is completely irrelevant for the purpose of a text widget.
[2] As the documentation explains, the CSS set with setDefaultStyleSheet() is only applied for new contents (set with setHtml(), through QTextCursor, etc.). That's why we only call setText() after setDefaultStyleSheet().

Q: How Do I Clear The Credentials In AWS Configure? A:

For mac users, run the below command to wipe the previous configurations with AWS cli to start afresh

rm -rf ~/.aws/credentials

rm -rf ~/.aws/config

Then I ran

aws login
